idiom_name: std::variant<...> + std::visit with an overloaded visitor
implementation_notes: Modern C++ expresses the sum directly: one struct per legal shape, std::variant over them, and std::visit with an overloaded visitor as the exhaustive consumer - a missing overload is a compile error instead of a wrong branch. std::variant is a type-safe union, so the tag and the payload are managed by the library, and the illegal combination simply has no type to inhabit; constructors of the shape structs (private fields plus validating factories) still carry the member invariants. Prefer this variant when the value is data: it is a value type, needs no allocation and keeps the closed set visible in one alias. Use std::monostate as the first alternative when a default-constructed state is needed, because a default-constructed variant holds its first alternative.
pitfalls: A variant can become valueless_by_exception when a type-changing assignment throws; std::visit and std::get then throw bad_variant_access, so keep the alternatives nothrow-movable or handle the state.

A default-constructed std::variant holds a value of its first alternative (and is not default-constructible at all if that alternative is not); put std::monostate first if 'not yet known' must be expressible.

The overloaded visitor only proves exhaustiveness while every alternative has a matching overload - an (auto&&) catch-all lambda silently swallows new alternatives, and implicit conversions can bind an alternative to the wrong overload.

variants.name: Closed class hierarchy with a protected constructor and final variants
variants.idiom_name: abstract base with protected constructor + final subclasses + visitor
variants.implementation_notes: Before C++17 (and wherever the model needs behaviour rather than plain data) the shapes are a class hierarchy: an abstract base with a protected constructor and derived classes marked final, usually consumed through a visitor whose abstract interface has one method per shape. C++ has no language mechanism to close a class hierarchy - final stops further derivation from each variant but the base can still be derived from unless its constructor is protected and the variants are its friends - so the closure is a convention kept by code review, and exhaustiveness lives in the Visitor interface (adding a shape means adding a method and breaking every visitor). Choose this variant when each state carries behaviour, or when the codebase predates C++17.
pitfalls: The base constructor must stay protected (or the variants friends): a public one lets any caller derive a new shape, and the 'closed' set silently reopens.
Holding variants by value slices them; store them behind a pointer or use the visitor over references, otherwise the derived payload is discarded in copies.
Adding a shape breaks the Visitor interface - which is the point, but only if no visitor defines a default method that silently absorbs the new case.
